title: Relational algebra
lead: From declarative SQL to relational operators, set semantics and composed query plans.

sections.title: Query languages and relational algebra
sections.html:
From SQL through calculus to algebra

The Student/Enrolled query has the logical expression πS.name(σE.cid='INF-11199'(Student ⋈S.sid=E.sid Enrolled)). A logical node names an operation; a physical node additionally names its algorithm, such as a tree scan or sort-merge join.

Relational calculus states that a result has a suitable enrolment witness. Algebra states a composition of operations producing the result. Codd’s theorem equates relational algebra with the domain-independent relational calculus, providing a constructive route from declarative conditions to executable operations. It does not mean every SQL extension is expressible in basic set algebra.

PDF pp. 1–5

Closure, types and multiplicities

Operators consume and return relations, so their outputs can feed further operators. Attribute schemas act as types: a later selection cannot refer to a column already projected away. Basic operators are selection, projection, rename, union, difference and Cartesian product; intersection and join can be derived.

Set relations contain no duplicate tuple. Bags retain multiplicities. A set projection removes duplicates; a SQL projection does not unless DISTINCT is requested. Choosing one semantics changes legal rewrites and aggregate results.

PDF pp. 6–7

sections.title: Selection and projection
sections.html:
Selection on the source relation

Let R(aid,bid) contain (a1,101), (a2,102), (a2,103), (a3,104). σaid='a2'(R) returns (a2,102) and (a2,103). Adding AND bid > 102 leaves (a2,103).

The result retains both attributes and their types. Selection chooses a subset of input tuples; it cannot invent duplicates under set semantics. AND/OR compose predicates, and a cascade of selections expresses conjunction.

PDF p. 8

Projection on the same data

πaid(R) returns {a1,a2,a3}; a2 appears once even though two source tuples have that aid. The output schema contains only aid. Under bag projection the result would retain two occurrences of a2.

This is why COUNT after SQL SELECT and after SELECT DISTINCT can differ. Duplicate removal requires work, typically sorting or hashing, and cannot be silently inserted into a bag query.

PDF p. 9

sections.title: Union, difference, product and renaming
sections.html:
Union and directional difference

For these slides use R={(a1,101),(a2,102),(a3,103)} and S={(a3,103),(a4,104),(a5,105)}. Their union has five tuples. R−S contains the first two R tuples; S−R contains (a4,104),(a5,105). Compute from the input rows; a mismatched value in an output figure is a source typo, not a new tuple.

Both operands must have compatible arity and corresponding types. Bag union adds multiplicities and bag difference uses max(mR − mS, 0). SQL UNION and EXCEPT remove duplicates unless ALL is specified and implemented by the engine.

PDF pp. 10–11

Product, renaming and intersection

For R={(a1,101),(a2,102),(a3,103)} and S={(b3,23),(b4,24)}, R×S has six combinations. Both bid attributes remain in the concatenated schema; rename them bid1 and bid2 or use unambiguous positions. Rename changes identifiers, not tuple values.

Intersection keeps tuples in both compatible inputs. For the preceding union example it is {(a3,103)} and equals R−(R−S). Under bag semantics INTERSECT ALL keeps min(mR,mS) occurrences. SQLite’s missing ALL variants are simulated only in the separate relational lab.

PDF pp. 12–14

sections.title: Joins and additional operators
sections.html:
Theta, equijoin and self-join

Theta join is selection on a product: R ⋈θ S = σθ(R×S). Equality-only conditions give an equijoin. The Student/Enrolled example matches sid and retains columns from both inputs; duplicate attribute names need renaming.

For a self-join Student₁.age < Student₂.age on Jones=18, Smith=23, Gold=21, the output pairs are Jones/Smith, Jones/Gold and Gold/Smith. The two copies must have separate variable/attribute identities. The result schema is the concatenation of both input schemas.

PDF pp. 15–17

Natural join and extended operators

For R(aid,bid)={(a1,101),(a2,102),(a3,103)} and S(bid,cid)={(101,c3),(101,c4),(105,c5)}, natural join returns (a1,101,c3),(a1,101,c4). It equates every shared field, then retains one copy of each shared attribute. Multiple matching S tuples yield multiple joined tuples.

Extended algebra names grouping/aggregation γ, duplicate elimination δ, sorting τ, assignment and division. Group selection corresponds to HAVING. Sorting introduces an order absent from pure unordered relational sets; division expresses “for every” membership conditions.

PDF pp. 18–20

quiz.question: If R has 3 rows and S has 4 rows, how many rows does R × S contain?
quiz.explanation: Each R row combines with every S row: 3×4=12. The Cartesian product has not yet applied a join condition; a later selection may reduce the number of pairs.
